issue.mint_text: Japan Mint (no mint mark on this type)

new.story: A Japanese 10 yen in bronze, dated Heisei 14 (2002), the fourteenth year of Emperor Akihito's reign. One side shows the Phoenix Hall of Byodoin temple in Uji, a thousand-year-old building so loved that it also appears on the 10,000 yen note. The other side frames a big 10 in bay laurel. Japan has struck this design, nearly unchanged, since 1951, and it is still the 10 yen in everyday pockets today. The collection already holds two Showa-era strikes of the same design from 1982 and 1988; this is its first Heisei one.
new.notes: Both sides photographed in the holder. Obverse: Phoenix Hall with the country name in kanji above and the value in kanji below. Reverse: big 10 inside a laurel wreath with the era date beneath in kanji, read as Heisei 14 (2002) glyph by glyph across enlarged and contrast-enhanced views; the year numeral is worn, so the year carries the caveat — era (Heisei) and the first three characters are clear, the fourth numeral reads as the boxed form of four. Bronze color and weight of the design rule out the aluminium 1 yen and brass 5 yen; the smooth edge and era name separate it from the collection's Showa strikes of the same type family.
